intro: Plenty of people step on a skateboard for the first time at thirty, forty or sixty. Others return to it after twenty years away, often because a child or a friend got a board. Adults bring real strengths to learning: patience, planning and the ability to explain what they feel. They also bring bodies that heal more slowly and lives that an injury can interrupt. This unit is about starting, or starting again, in a way that respects both.

The first chapter covers what to do before the first real roll: protective gear and how to fit it, why wrist guards matter so much, a short warm-up, choosing a steady board and practicing falls on grass. It ends with where and when to skate and how to set small goals. The second chapter covers how adults actually learn a movement, how to work with fear instead of against it, how to learn with a coach, a crew or a child, and how to track progress with notes and video.

By the end you will be able to fit a helmet and pads, plan a warm-up, choose a board for your goals, fall small, find your stance, break a trick like the kickturn into steps and design a weekly practice plan you can keep. You will also be able to explain the science behind those choices, from impact speed to the stages of motor learning.
bigQuestion: How can an adult start or return to skateboarding safely and keep getting better for years?

timeline.t: Larry Stevenson's Makaha begins selling skateboards in California
First National Skateboard Championships in Anaheim; Patti McGee is women's champion
Fitts and Posner describe three stages of learning a physical skill
Larry Stevenson is granted a patent for a kicktail design
Frank Nasworthy's urethane Cadillac Wheels give a smoother, grippier ride
Carlsbad Skatepark and Skateboard City open as early purpose-built parks
Albert Bandura publishes his theory of self-efficacy
The Tony Hawk Foundation forms to help communities build public skateparks
Oliver Percovich founds Skateistan in Kabul, Afghanistan
The IOC adds skateboarding to the Olympic Games
Skateboarding debuts at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, held a year late

words.d: equipment worn to lower injury in a fall, such as a helmet, wrist guards, knee pads and elbow pads
gloves or sleeves with a stiff palm-side splint that protect the wrist in a fall
controlled movements through a range of motion that prepare the body for activity
a scale that measures wheel hardness; skate wheels run from about 78A (soft) to about 101A (hard)
a board with large, soft wheels made for smooth rolling and getting around
the point where a body's weight is balanced; lowering it makes a fall shorter and slower
which foot a skater keeps in front: regular (left) or goofy (right)
a small, specific action you control and can complete in one session
practice spread across several shorter sessions instead of one long one
a turn made by pressing the tail, lifting the front wheels and pivoting on the back wheels
a person's belief that they can succeed at a specific task
the sense of where your body parts are and how they move, without looking

test.q: Why does an adult beginner need protection even more than a child?
choices: Adult bodies usually heal more slowly
test.why: Slower healing means an adult injury usually costs more time.

test.q: How many fingers should fit between your eyebrows and the front of a fitted helmet?
test.why: About two finger-widths keeps the forehead covered without blocking sight.

test.q: What does the splint in a wrist guard do?
choices: Makes the hand grip the ground
Lets the palm slide and stops the wrist bending too far back
test.why: The palm-side splint protects the wrist in a fall on an outstretched hand.

test.q: About what durometer rating is a soft cruising wheel?
test.why: Soft wheels are about 78A; hard park wheels are about 99A to 101A.

test.q: Which board is built mainly for smooth rolling and getting around?
choices: A narrow street deck with hard wheels
test.why: Cruisers have big, soft wheels for paths and streets.

test.q: Why does crouching low make a fall safer?
choices: It lowers the center of mass, so you land slower
test.why: A shorter drop gives a lower impact speed, as v = √(2gh) shows.

test.q: Which foot goes over the front bolts when you stand on a board?
test.why: The front foot covers the front bolts and the back foot covers the back bolts.

test.q: Which stance has the right foot in front?
test.why: Goofy is right foot forward; regular is left foot forward.

test.q: What is snaking at a skatepark?
choices: Cutting in front of someone else's turn
test.why: Snaking is slang for taking someone's turn.

test.q: Which stage of motor learning lets a skill run mostly on its own?
test.why: In the autonomous stage the skill needs little conscious attention.

test.q: What is the most common mistake when first learning a kickturn?
choices: Pressing the tail too hard so the board shoots forward
test.why: Too hard a press tips you back; a lighter press with bent knees fixes it.

test.q: What is the strongest source of self-efficacy, according to Albert Bandura?
What does the American Academy of Pediatrics advise for children under 5?
test.why: The AAP advises that children under 5 should not ride skateboards.

test.q: A center of mass drops 0.5 m. Using v = √(2gh) with g = 9.8 m/s², about how fast does it land?
test.why: 2 × 9.8 × 0.5 = 9.8, and the square root of 9.8 is about 3.13 m/s.

test.q: A trick takes 0.5 seconds. How many frames does it fill at 240 frames per second?

write.prompt: Write a four-week plan for an adult starting to skate. Explain the gear and how to fit it, your falling drills and the physics of why crouching low helps, your weekly sessions and why they are short and frequent, and the small goals you will track.
tips: Name each piece of gear and one fit check for it.
Show the impact-speed arithmetic for a tall fall and a crouched fall.
Use front foot and back foot, never left and right.
Give each week one measurable process goal.
Say how you will handle fear or a bad day.
